questions.text: Any set of Boolean operation that is sufficient to represent all Boolean expression is said to be complete. Which of the following is not complete ?
questions.solution:
Without NOT, AND and OR can only build monotone functions, so they cannot express [latex]\bar x[/latex]. {AND, NOT}, {OR, NOT} and {NOR} are all functionally complete.

Answer: {AND, OR}

questions.text: A computer uses ternary system instead of the traditional systen, An n bit string in the binary system will occupy
questions.solution:
n bits represent [latex]2^n[/latex] values. With k ternary digits we need [latex]3^k=2^n\Rightarrow k=n\log_32[/latex].

Answer: [latex]n\log_32[/latex] ternary digits

questions.text: Given [latex]\sqrt{224_{r}}=13_{r}[/latex] the value of radix r is
questions.solution:
[latex](13_r)^2=(r+3)^2=r^2+6r+9[/latex] and [latex]224_r=2r^2+2r+4[/latex].
[latex]2r^2+2r+4=r^2+6r+9\Rightarrow r^2-4r-5=0\Rightarrow r=5[/latex]

Answer: 5

questions.text: In the diagram above, the inverter (NOT gate) and the AND-gates labeled 1 and 2 have delays of 9, 10 and 12 nanoseconds (ns), respectively. Wire delays are negligible. For certain values a and c, together with certain transition of b, a glitch (spurious output) is generated for a short time, after which the output assumes its correct value. The duration of glitch is:
questions.solution:
Output = [latex]a\bar b+bc[/latex]. Take a = c = 1 and let b go from 1 to 0:
- gate 2 (bc) drops to 0 after 12 ns
- gate 1 ([latex]a\bar b[/latex]) rises to 1 only after the inverter and gate 1: 9 + 10 = 19 ns

Between 12 and 19 ns both inputs of the OR are 0, so the output glitches to 0 for 19 [latex]-[/latex] 12 = 7 ns.

Answer: 7 ns

questions.text: If a variable can take only integral values from 0 to n, where n is an integer, then the variable can be represented as a bit-field whose width is (the log in the answer are to the base 2, and [latex]\lceil\log n\rceil[/latex] means the floor of [latex]\log_{}{n}[/latex] )
questions.solution:
Values 0 to n need [latex]\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor+1[/latex] bits. The options use ceiling brackets, which overestimate in general: e.g. n = 5 needs 3 bits (0-7), but [latex]\lceil\log_25\rceil+1=4[/latex]. So none of the given formulas is exact.

Answer: None of the above
